extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of comparative mythology / folklore (beginners to intermediate)
extracted.subtask_description: A set of conceptual criteria and classificatory principles used by students and critics of myth to identify, date, classify, and explain myths and their transformations across cultures. Includes definitions (totemism, polytheism, monotheism), tests of authenticity, causes of change, and taxonomy of myth types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Totemism definition and identifying features
rubrics_metrics.description: The totem is an animal, plant, or inanimate object connected traditionally with a certain social group which takes its name from the totem or uses it as a symbol; members suppose themselves descended from or related to the totem and there is a magico-religious bond; the totem may not be eaten except ceremonially and at stated seasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jupiter as swan (Roman), Egyptian animal-headed gods, swine-gods of ancient Britons, modern tribal taboos (e.g., some Red Indians not eating beaver or raccoon). Use presence of descent-claims, symbolic use, magico-religious bond, and food-taboo as indicators of totemic relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polytheism emergence and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Polytheism is a condition with a multiplicity of gods often arranged in a hierarchy resembling the social polity of the people; polytheistic pantheons form by deities shedding attributes and variants that become personalized gods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for processes such as attribute-shedding, localization of gods (local variants), priestly grouping of town gods into ranked pantheons, absorption/adoption of foreign deities and modification by conquest, trade, or priestly influence (Egyptian examples given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Monotheism emergence pathways and characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Monotheism (worship of one god) may emerge from polytheism by one god becoming dominant through miracles, conquest, priestly enterprise, dynastic association, or absorption of lesser gods; monotheistic gods often have the right to pardon sin and embody a higher moral standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing a religion's development, consider political/dynastic factors, priestly activity, moral/ethical evolution, or miraculous claims as drivers for transition from polytheism to monotheism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of mythic evolution (animistic → personified → deity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mythical figures may evolve in stages: an animistic conception (a thing endowed with personality) can become a tale-hero and later a god (e.g., Blue Jay: bird as person → tale-hero → vanquisher of death; Uitzilopochtli: bird-guided leader → full national war-god).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use narrative sequence and retention of earlier attributes (bird-like traits in a later human god) to trace evolutionary stages; persistent features (name meanings, rites) support stage-wise development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of mythic change
rubrics_metrics.description: Four principal causes: (1) evolution/growth of theological ideas; (2) growth of sacred/ethical ideas raising moral objections to earlier elements; (3) adventitious circumstances such as racial idiosyncrasy or fusion of myths; (4) survival of myth after official religious demise leading to secret celebration and degeneration into magic/folk-tale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining alterations in a myth, evaluate theological shifts, moral/ethical pressures, demographic or cultural fusions, and the social context in which a myth survives or is practiced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing of myths by later redactors
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths may be 'edited' wholesale by later scribes/mithographers who add, split, or recombine concepts (e.g., Babylonian cosmogony: an original single concept of 'the deep' rendered into multiple deities such as Apsu, Tiawath, Mummu, Kingu).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signs of late editing include sudden additions of new deities, internal inconsistencies or narrative discontinuities, and theological redaction that creates polities (trinities) from originally singular concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of myth by cosmic/social problem addressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief divisions of myth correspond to fundamental questions posed by the universe: origin of world, origin of man, origin of arts, star myths, sun/moon myths, myths of death, fire-stealing, hero myths, taboo myths, beast myths, underworld journeys, and myths explaining customs/rites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the function or explanatory target of a tale (what it seeks to explain) as the primary classificatory criterion; many myths will fit into these thematic heads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution: diffusion vs spontaneous origin criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarities between myths across wide areas may reflect wide dissemination (via slaves, intermarriage, trade, capture) or independent spontaneous creation; isolation (e.g., Australia, America) complicates diffusion theories and suggests antiquity or independent origin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess historical contact mechanisms and geographic/isolation constraints; consider whether dissemination over the relevant time/depth is plausible, and whether similar environmental or cognitive pressures could produce analogous myths independently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators of mythic sophistication
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths show 'sophistication' when coloured by contact with higher civilization; marked ethical contrasts (sharp good/evil) in primitive myths often indicate later influence by a superior culture or agents of sophistication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a primitive tradition exhibits moral refinement or literary embellishment atypical for its context, suspect external influence or accelerated development; but allow for independent moral evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism and relative antiquity: simplicity vs literary embellishment
rubrics_metrics.description: The more simple and archaic the characteristics of a myth (reflecting early social states), the greater the likelihood of its antiquity; more literary, embellished, or cunningly told myths are generally later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use stylistic simplicity, lack of literary ornament, and retention of archaic circumstances as indicators of greater antiquity; conversely, literary grace and elaborate plot suggest later composition or redaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of recurrence as proof of authenticity/antiquity
rubrics_metrics.description: If a tale possessing the same elements is discovered in several different parts of the world, coincidence is unlikely and recurrence supports genealogical connection or great antiquity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the recurrence test cautiously: multiple independent occurrences of the same tale-structure increase confidence in an ancient or disseminated origin; combine with diffusion plausibility and contextual evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary (renovated) myths indicator
rubrics_metrics.description: When myth is 'renovated,' cleansed, cast into literary form, or otherwise altered it is known as 'secondary' myth — i.e., not the original aboriginal product but a later, edited state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs of literary stylization, clerical/priestly purification, moralizing, or explicit alignment with newer theological systems to label a myth 'secondary.' Cross-reference with evidence of earlier oral forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animism/animatism as a foundational diagnostic
rubrics_metrics.description: Animism is the doctrine of spiritual beings incl. human souls (often extended to animatism: the idea that much of the inanimate kingdom has intelligence/volition); many myths possess an animistic basis, and identification of animistic elements helps interpret myth origins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use presence of personification of natural objects, spirits inhabiting things, and attribution of will/intelligence to non-human entities as evidence of animistic foundations for a myth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation of myth to history and oral tradition criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Myth must not be identified with history; many myths existed long as oral tradition before being written, and later attachment to historical events or persons can preserve a myth into historic periods but also distort origin interpretations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between oral-origin mythic plot and later historical accretions; treat apparent historical references as possible later re-interpretations rather than proof of historic truth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms of myth transmission and fusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Myths may change through migration, conquest, priestly identification (identifying alien gods with native ones), trade, and cultural contact, leading to fusion, adoption, or alteration of mythic elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When tracing a myth's variants, evaluate historical contacts, priestly/elite roles in identification and syncretism, and sociopolitical factors that favour fusion or adoption of foreign mythic elements.
